conceptTag: Why are customers leaving a gym?
readerTitle: Members are quitting the gym. Where do you look first?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (동네 헬스장, 식당 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: '고객이 떠난다'는 문제가 아니라 증상이다. 누가, 언제부터, 무엇과 비교해 떠나는지 정의하고 쪼개면 어디를 볼지가 저절로 좁혀진다.
misconception: 이탈이 늘면 바로 할인이나 설문, 새 기능 같은 해결책부터 내놓아야 한다. 전체 숫자만 보면 원인을 알 수 있다.

sources.text: 모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 차트 계산 확인: 지난달 해지 14 + 10 + 6 = 30, 이번 달 32 + 12 + 6 = 50. 증가분 20 중 가입 3개월 미만 회원이 +18(90%), 3~12개월 +2, 1년 이상 0.
헬스장이 2월에 무료 트레이너 첫 세션을 없앴다는 설정은 설명용 가상 사례입니다. 실제 업계 통계나 연구를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Members are quitting the gym. Where do you look first?
body: Maya owns a neighborhood gym with about 1,000 members. For a year, around 30 people cancelled each month. This month, 50 did.
Her team has ideas already: a discount, new machines, longer hours. Each idea costs money. None of them starts with a clear picture of who is leaving.

image.label: Gym front desk with a growing stack of cancellation forms
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 동네 헬스장 프런트 데스크 위에 해지 신청서가 쌓여 있고, 사장이 팔짱을 끼고 바라봄. 뒤로 운동 기구가 흐릿하게 보임. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: What should Maya do first?
body: Cancellations jumped from 30 to 50 in one month. Maya has a staff meeting tomorrow and wants to act fast.

options.text: Offer 20% off to anyone who tries to cancel
options.feedback: It may slow cancellations for a while, but it treats a symptom she hasn't defined. She could lose margin on every member and never learn the cause.

options.text: Send every member a survey about what they'd like improved
options.feedback: Listening is good, but most answers will come from people who are staying. It gathers opinions before the question is clear.

options.text: Pin down who is leaving, since when, and compared to what
options.feedback: This is **defining the problem first**. A sharper question costs little and tells her where to spend effort.

cards.title: Turn a worry into a question.
body: "Customers are leaving" feels like a problem, but it points nowhere. Maya rewrites it: **"Monthly cancellations rose from 30 to 50 this month. Which members are leaving, and what changed for them?"**
Now she has a starting number, a time window and a target to explain: 20 extra cancellations. Any idea that can't explain those 20 can wait.

image.label: A vague sentence rewritten into a precise question
image.brief: 메모지 두 장 비교. 왼쪽 "Customers are leaving"에 줄이 그어져 있고, 오른쪽에 "30 → 50 cancellations this month. Who? What changed?"가 또렷하게 적힘. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일.

cards.title: Split the 50 by how long people had been members.
body: Maya splits cancellations into three groups that add up to the whole: new, middle and long-time members.
cards.callout: 18 of the 20 extra cancellations came from members who joined in the last three months.

cards.title: Now where should Maya look?
body: Long-time members are leaving at the same rate as before. New members are not.

options.text: What changed in a new member's first weeks recently
options.feedback: Breaking the problem into parts put 90% of the increase in one group. Looking there first is the cheapest path to the cause.

options.text: The old equipment long-time members keep complaining about
options.feedback: The complaints may be real, but that group's cancellations didn't move. Fixing it spends money on a problem that isn't this one.

options.text: All three groups equally, to be thorough
options.feedback: Thorough, but slow. Splitting the problem is useful precisely because it tells you where *not* to look yet.

cards.title: One small cut, one big leak.
body: Maya checks the new-member journey step by step: sign-up, first visit, first month. In February, to save costs, the gym had dropped its free first session with a trainer.
Many recent joiners came once or twice, felt lost, and stopped coming. Weeks later they cancelled. Bringing back a shorter intro session costs far less than a discount for everyone.

cards.title: The first split may not be the right one.
body: Maya got lucky: tenure revealed the pattern on the first try. Often it won't. Try a few cuts, such as time of day, plan type or location, and keep the parts adding up to the whole so nothing hides in a gap.
And a split shows *where* the change is, not *why*. She still had to look at what happened to those members before acting.

cards.title: Now it's restaurant booking software.
body: You sell reservation software to restaurants on a monthly plan. Over two months, cancellations doubled. Your team wants to rush out the most-requested feature. What's your first move?

options.text: Build the most-requested feature as fast as possible
options.feedback: Requests come mostly from customers who stay. You'd spend months of engineering without knowing whether it touches the restaurants that left.

options.text: Split cancellations by sign-up date, plan and restaurant size, and compare with before
options.feedback: This **defines the problem** and **breaks it into parts** at once. If the jump sits in one group, you know where to dig.

options.text: Call the five biggest restaurants that cancelled
options.feedback: You'll hear useful stories, but five large accounts may not represent the dozens of small ones that left. Calls work better after the split shows who to call.

cards.title: Before fixing "leaving," find out who is leaving.
body: This lesson used two tools: **define the problem first** (a number, a time window, a comparison) and **break it into parts** that add up to the whole. Together they shrank a vague worry into one place to look.
**Try it today:** take one number you're worried about. Write it as "X changed from A to B since when," then split it into three groups that add up to the total.
